cases.title: Stroke Rehabilitation: Outcome-Driven Plan Revision and Fieldwork Mentorship
cases.vignette:
Mr. Delgado is a 68-year-old man admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation unit 12 days ago following a left hemisphere ischemic stroke. He presents with right hemiplegia, expressive aphasia, and moderate deficits in self-care performance. Prior to admission, he was independent in all activities of daily living and lived alone in a single-story home. He communicates preferences reliably through gestures and yes/no responses. His adult daughter attends therapy sessions when her work schedule permits.

Over the past week, the treating occupational therapist (OT) has been implementing a compensatory approach to upper-extremity dressing and grooming retraining. Upon reviewing Mr. Delgado's Functional Independence Measure (FIM) scores at the two-week mark, the OT identifies minimal functional gains. The OT recently reviewed a systematic review indicating that task-specific training combined with graded repetition produces superior upper-extremity outcomes compared to compensatory strategies alone for clients with moderate paresis at this stage of recovery. The rehabilitation unit has also recently welcomed a Level II fieldwork student, who will begin co-treating with the OT beginning next week.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist is beginning services with a 45-year-old adult recovering from a stroke. The therapist wants to identify the client's self-perceived occupational performance problems, their importance to the client, and establish a baseline for measuring outcomes over time. Which assessment is MOST appropriate?
questions.correct_rationale: The COPM is a client-centered, semi-structured interview that asks clients to identify occupational performance problems across self-care, productivity, and leisure, then rate each problem on importance, perceived performance, and satisfaction (each on a 1–10 scale). This dual focus — capturing what matters to the client and producing scored baselines — makes it specifically designed for client-identified goal-setting and detection of clinically meaningful change over time, fulfilling all three requirements in the stem.
questions.core_concept: The Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) operationalizes client-centered practice by transferring problem identification and prioritization to the client rather than the clinician. It is the standard OT tool when the clinical goal is to measure self-perceived occupational performance and satisfaction as outcomes, because it is occupation-based, individualized, and sensitive to change.
questions.explain_differently: Picture handing the client a blank "problem list" and asking them to fill it in — that is the COPM. Every other tool on this list has the therapist or a standardized checklist deciding what to measure. The COPM is unique because the client names what they struggle with, scores how important it is, and then scores how well they think they are doing it. That combination of client voice plus scored outcomes is exactly what the stem is asking for.
questions.topic: Occupational Performance Assessment — Client-Centered Outcome Measurement

options.label: A
options.text: Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)

options.label: B
options.text: Barthel Index
options.incorrect_rationale: The Barthel Index measures observer-rated ADL independence but does not capture the client's subjective perception of performance problems or their personal priorities.

options.label: C
options.text: Functional Independence Measure (FIM)
options.incorrect_rationale: The FIM rates functional independence across 18 items from the clinician's perspective and does not elicit the client's self-perception of performance or satisfaction with meaningful occupations.

options.label: D
options.text: Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE)
options.incorrect_rationale: The MMSE is a cognitive screening tool; it does not assess occupational performance, client-identified priorities, or satisfaction with daily activities.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist conducts a home assessment with a First Nations elder who sustained a hip fracture and is preparing for discharge. The elder's adult daughter is present and explains that the family has arranged for a traditional healer to visit weekly. The elder nods as his daughter speaks but has not yet expressed his own goals. Which action should the occupational therapist take FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: Acknowledging the family's plan first demonstrates respect for collective decision-making practices that are normative in many Indigenous communities. Then directly and openly inviting the elder to articulate his own meaning and goals ensures the client's voice is centred rather than mediated through a family member, fulfilling both cultural safety and client-centred principles simultaneously. This sequence gathers essential occupational performance data from the person whose participation is the focus of intervention.
questions.core_concept: Cultural safety in OT practice requires the therapist to actively create conditions in which clients from marginalized or Indigenous communities can share their perspectives without coercion or judgment. In collectivist cultural frameworks, family presence and shared decision-making are normative and must be respected rather than dismantled; the therapist's role is to honour both relational structures and the individual client's voice.
questions.explain_differently: Think of it like being a guest in someone else's household. You don't rearrange the furniture (remove the daughter) or ignore the homeowner (proceed without asking him) — you greet everyone respectfully, then turn to the person whose home it is and ask, "What matters most to you here?" Option C does exactly that: it honours the family structure already in the room and then opens the door for the elder himself to speak.
questions.topic: Cultural safety and client-centred goal-setting with Indigenous older adults

options.label: A
options.text: Proceed with the standard home safety assessment and document the family's plan for the traditional healer in the clinical notes.
options.incorrect_rationale: Proceeding with assessment before establishing the elder's own priorities treats the family report as sufficient and bypasses the client's direct voice, which is inconsistent with client-centred practice.

options.label: B
options.text: Acknowledge the family's plan, then invite the elder directly to describe what returning to his home life means to him.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the daughter to step out of the room so the elder can express his personal goals without family influence.
options.incorrect_rationale: Removing the family without the client's invitation imposes an individualistic Western norm onto a setting where collective family involvement may be culturally appropriate and expected, which is culturally unsafe.

options.label: D
options.text: Contact the traditional healer to align healing practices with the OT discharge goals before beginning the assessment.
options.incorrect_rationale: Coordinating with the traditional healer is a valuable step but is premature before the therapist has first established what the elder himself wants from the return home.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist working in an inpatient rehabilitation unit has completed a standardized functional assessment showing that a client recovering from a traumatic brain injury scores at a maximal assistance level for all instrumental ADLs and demonstrates poor safety awareness on objective testing. During the weekly interdisciplinary team meeting, the physiatrist announces a discharge date in three days because insurance authorization has been exhausted. The client, who retains decision-making capacity, states he wants to go home. His spouse reports feeling "too overwhelmed" to provide full-time caregiving and has not been trained in any assist techniques. The OT believes discharge in three days poses a serious safety risk. Which action should the OT take FIRST?
questions.correct_rationale: The OT is currently inside the interprofessional forum where the discharge decision is being reached. Interprofessional collaboration competencies require that each discipline contribute discipline-specific, evidence-based findings at the point of team decision-making — not after the fact. Presenting standardized, objective data (rather than opinion) gives the team actionable clinical information, honors the OT's professional accountability to client safety, and initiates collaborative problem-solving (e.g., extended stay, transitional care unit, intensive caregiver training) within the appropriate channel. All other options either skip a step, delay advocacy, or route around the team structure prematurely.
questions.core_concept: Interprofessional advocacy requires OTs to raise evidence-based safety concerns within the shared team forum at the moment the decision is being made, using objective, standardized data rather than subjective opinion. Raising concerns after the meeting or bypassing the team to escalate elsewhere first undermines collaborative practice standards and the OT's professional accountability for client safety.
questions.explain_differently: Picture the team meeting as the one open window where all clinical voices can change the outcome in real time. The OT holds a key — objective, standardized assessment data that no other discipline collected. Waiting to slip a note under the door after the meeting closes, or going directly to the insurance company or the chart, means the window has already shut. Speaking up now, with data in hand, is not confrontation — it is exactly what interprofessional teams are designed to do: integrate each discipline's unique findings before locking in a plan.
questions.topic: Interprofessional Team Communication and Clinical Advocacy at Discharge Planning

options.label: A
options.text: Contact the insurance company's utilization review department directly to request a continued-stay authorization on behalf of the client.
options.incorrect_rationale: Contacting the insurer directly bypasses the interprofessional team and is typically the responsibility of the case manager or social worker; the OT should work through the team structure before escalating outside it.

options.label: B
options.text: Document the OT's clinical concerns thoroughly in the medical record and request that the physiatrist review them before finalizing the discharge date.
options.incorrect_rationale: Charting is necessary but passive; because the OT is already present in the decision-making forum, deferring to a written note after the meeting forfeits the immediate opportunity for real-time interprofessional advocacy.

options.label: C
options.text: Present the objective functional assessment scores and specific safety concerns to the team during the current meeting, and propose that discharge alternatives be formally discussed before the date is finalized.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer.

options.label: D
options.text: Arrange a home visit before the next team meeting to assess environmental safety and evaluate caregiver feasibility before weighing in on the discharge plan.
options.incorrect_rationale: A home visit may be a useful later step, but it is not feasible within a three-day window as a first action, and it delays the OT's obligation to raise safety concerns in the current clinical forum where the decision is actively being made.

questions.stem: An occupational therapist provides home health services to a 72-year-old client with mild cognitive impairment who lives alone. During a session, the client discloses that their adult son has been withdrawing money from the client's bank account without permission. The client becomes tearful and says, "Please don't tell anyone — he is all I have, and I don't want to get him in trouble." The client is alert, oriented to person and place, and demonstrates insight into the situation. What is the OT's most appropriate next action?
questions.correct_rationale: Financial exploitation of a vulnerable adult constitutes elder abuse under mandatory reporting statutes in all U.S. jurisdictions. OT practitioners are designated mandated reporters, meaning the legal obligation to report reasonable suspicion of abuse to Adult Protective Services (APS) is triggered regardless of client consent or confidentiality preferences. Informing the client before reporting respects autonomy and therapeutic alliance while fulfilling the legal duty. The client's cognitive status and insight do not remove the OT's reporting obligation; mandatory reporting laws exist precisely because clients in exploitative situations often resist disclosure out of fear or loyalty.
questions.core_concept: Mandatory reporting statutes designate OT practitioners as mandated reporters who must report reasonable suspicion of elder abuse, neglect, or financial exploitation to protective authorities. This legal duty is non-discretionary and overrides both client requests for confidentiality and professional deference to other disciplines. Distinguishing when mandatory reporting obligations arise — and acting on them promptly — is a foundational professional responsibility competency.
questions.explain_differently: Imagine the law has already made this decision for the clinician. For most clinical choices, the OT weighs evidence and exercises judgment. Mandatory reporting is different: the moment there is reasonable suspicion of abuse of a vulnerable adult, the law removes that discretion and requires action. The client's wish for secrecy and the OT's empathy for the family relationship are real and valid feelings — but they are not factors the law permits the OT to weigh against reporting. The OT can be compassionate in how they explain the report to the client, but the report itself is not optional.
questions.topic: Mandatory Reporting of Elder Abuse and Financial Exploitation

options.label: A
options.text: Honor the client's request, document the disclosure in the medical record, and monitor the situation during future visits.
options.incorrect_rationale: Mandatory reporting laws supersede client confidentiality in cases of suspected abuse or exploitation; documentation alone does not fulfill the OT's legal duty to report, and delaying action may leave the client at continued risk.

options.label: B
options.text: Contact the son directly to discuss the client's concerns and attempt to mediate a resolution between them.
options.incorrect_rationale: Alerting an alleged perpetrator can escalate danger to the client, compromise a future protective investigation, and falls outside the OT's professional role; the OT is not a mediator in abuse situations.

options.label: C
options.text: Consult the supervising physician and defer any external reporting until clinical guidance is received.
options.incorrect_rationale: Mandatory reporting is a direct legal obligation of the individual OT practitioner; it is not contingent on physician authorization or interdisciplinary consultation, and deferring the report could cause harmful delay.

options.label: D
options.text: Explain to the client that the situation must be reported to Adult Protective Services, then submit a mandatory report.

questions.stem: Based on Mr. Delgado's FIM data showing minimal functional gains and the OT's review of current systematic review evidence, what is the OT's BEST next step in his care?
questions.correct_rationale: Evidence-based practice requires integrating the best available research evidence with clinical outcome data and individual client factors. The FIM reveals a functional plateau under the current compensatory approach, and the systematic review directly supports task-specific training with graded repetition for clients with Mr. Delgado's profile. Modifying the treatment plan to align with this evidence is the appropriate professional response and reflects both quality improvement and outcome-driven clinical decision-making.
questions.core_concept: Evidence-based practice in OT integrates current best research evidence with standardized outcome measurement and client-specific factors to guide treatment planning. When outcome data indicate insufficient progress, the clinician is professionally obligated to revise the intervention approach rather than continue a plan that is not producing meaningful change.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the FIM as the OT's report card on the intervention — and right now the grade is failing. If you also know from research that a different teaching strategy works better for this type of student, the right move is to switch strategies, not to keep using the same one and hope something changes. Clinging to an approach that both the data and the evidence argue against is not reflective practice; it is inertia.
questions.topic: Evidence-Based Practice and Outcome-Driven Plan Modification

options.label: A
options.text: Revise the treatment plan to incorporate task-specific training with graded repetition, consistent with the current systematic review evidence.
options.incorrect_rationale: This is the correct answer and does not require an incorrect rationale.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue the compensatory approach for two additional weeks to allow more time for the current plan to demonstrate effect.
options.incorrect_rationale: Persisting with an approach that outcome data show is ineffective, without incorporating available evidence, does not reflect evidence-based or quality improvement practice.

options.label: C
options.text: Discontinue occupational therapy services and refer Mr. Delgado to home health, given the plateau in functional gains.
options.incorrect_rationale: A plateau under the current approach does not indicate discharge readiness; the client has unmet functional goals and evidence supports a more effective alternative intervention.

options.label: D
options.text: Request a physiatrist consultation to evaluate whether Mr. Delgado's neurological status has changed before making any modifications to the intervention plan.
options.incorrect_rationale: A neurological consultation is not indicated without clinical signs of neurological change; the OT holds professional authority and responsibility to modify intervention approaches based on outcome data and best evidence.

questions.stem: During a co-treatment dressing session, the Level II fieldwork student recommends continuing Mr. Delgado's compensatory dressing approach, stating he is "more comfortable" with those techniques. The supervising OT notes that Mr. Delgado's FIM self-care scores have plateaued for three consecutive weeks and that the systematic review evidence the team reviewed last week consistently favors task-specific training for motor recovery in patients with ischemic stroke. Which of the following actions BEST reflects the supervising OT's role as a fieldwork educator?
questions.correct_rationale: ACOTE standards require Level II fieldwork supervisors to provide direct, ongoing, and formative feedback rather than deferring guidance to scheduled evaluations. Structured post-session feedback anchored to an observable clinical event — the student's preference for compensatory techniques despite a measurable FIM plateau and contradicting systematic-review evidence — develops the student's evidence-based clinical reasoning while protecting Mr. Delgado's right to best-practice care. Collaboratively revising the plan models the OT process and fulfills the educator role more completely than any unilateral or delayed action.
questions.core_concept: Level II fieldwork educators are obligated by ACOTE standards to deliver timely, structured, formative feedback tied to observable clinical events, and to guide students in integrating current evidence into client-centered intervention planning.
questions.explain_differently: Think of the fieldwork educator's role as a two-track responsibility: keeping the client on the most evidence-supported path while simultaneously teaching the student why that path is correct. When the student's comfort with a familiar technique conflicts with objective outcome data (FIM plateau) and current evidence (systematic review favoring task-specific training), the educator's best move is a structured debrief that makes the student do the reasoning — not a silent override, not a delayed midterm note, and not unsupervised continuation. The feedback must be timely (post-session, not at midterm), structured (linked to specific observable data), and collaborative (the student builds the rationale, not just receives an answer).
questions.topic: Fieldwork Education and Professional Supervision in Occupational Therapy

options.label: A
options.text: Direct the student to implement the task-specific training protocol immediately and without discussion so that Mr. Delgado receives the most evidence-supported intervention without further delay.
options.incorrect_rationale: Bypassing the educational dialogue prioritizes immediate protocol compliance over developing the student's clinical reasoning, which is the primary obligation of the fieldwork-educator role and is required for the student to integrate evidence into future independent practice.

options.label: B
options.text: Defer all feedback on the student's clinical reasoning to the formal midterm evaluation form, allowing the student sufficient independent time to recognize the evidence-practice discrepancy before it is discussed.
options.incorrect_rationale: Withholding timely, formative feedback violates ACOTE Level II fieldwork standards, allows the evidence-practice gap to persist uncorrected across multiple sessions, and places Mr. Delgado at continued risk of a suboptimal functional outcome.

options.label: C
options.text: Provide structured, post-session feedback that guides the student to reconcile the systematic-review evidence with Mr. Delgado's three-week FIM plateau and collaboratively develop a rationale for revising the intervention plan.

options.label: D
options.text: Allow the student to continue leading dressing sessions with the compensatory approach while the OT monitors unobtrusively from outside the room to avoid undermining the student's developing clinical confidence.
options.incorrect_rationale: Permitting an approach that conflicts with current evidence and an objective plateau in client progress, without direct supervisory feedback, subordinates client safety and evidence-based practice to the student's comfort — the inverse of the fieldwork educator's professional responsibility.
